name: Prefrontal Cortex (Dorsolateral, Ventromedial, Orbitofrontal)
function: Executive functioning, reasoning, planning, problem-solving, personality characteristics, decision-making, emotional/impulse regulation, working memory, and recognition of smell.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Apathy, severe impulsivity, poor risk assessment, emotional blunting, utilization behavior, and profound personality alterations (e.g., Phineas Gage pattern).

name: Broca's Area (Inferior Frontal Gyrus)
function: Speech production, articulation, motor planning of expression, and complex grammatical syntax generation.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Non-fluent, slow, fragmented, telegraphic speech output with agrammatism; writing is similarly affected, though speech comprehension remains mostly intact.

name: Primary Motor Cortex (Precentral Gyrus)
function: Controls voluntary motor movements throughout the body via topographically organized corticospinal tract execution.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Weakness, loss of voluntary fine motor control, or spastic paralysis on the opposite side of the body.

name: Primary Somatosensory Cortex (Postcentral Gyrus)
function: Processes somatosensory input including touch, temperature, pressure, proprioception, and pain interpretation.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Loss of tactile awareness, impaired temperature discrimination, and inability to identify objects by touch alone on the opposite side of the body.

name: Posterior Parietal Cortex & Spatial Processing Zone
function: Visuospatial relationships, body schema orientation in space (where body is relative to environment), object identification, calculation, and reading.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Right lesion causes left side spatial neglect. Left hemisphere damage to BA 39/40 causes Gerstmann Syndrome: acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and right-left confusion.

name: Wernicke's Area (Superior Temporal / Parietal Region)
function: Language comprehension, decoding spoken and written speech, and semantic interpretation.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Fluent but meaningless speech output ('word salad'), verbal paraphasias, neologisms, and severe impairment in language comprehension.

name: Primary Auditory Cortex (Heschl's Gyrus)
function: Tonotopic processing of auditory signals including frequency, pitch, volume, musical rhythm, and sound localization.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Inability to perceive complex environmental sounds or recognize familiar audio patterns despite intact inner ear pathways.

name: Inferior Temporal Cortex & Fusiform Gyrus
function: High-level visual object recognition, facial identification, category representation, and short-term memory integration.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Inability to recognize familiar faces (prosopagnosia) or identify common objects visually despite intact basic vision.

name: Primary Visual Cortex (V1 / Striate Cortex)
function: Primary visual processing center of the brain, handling spatial contrast, orientation, motion, and visual field topography.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Loss of visual field awareness (e.g., hemianopia) or cortical blindness, sometimes with denial of visual deficit (Anton-Babinski syndrome).

name: Thalamus
function: Central relay station passing sensory (all except olfaction) and motor signals to the cerebral cortex; regulates cortical arousal and consciousness.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Contralateral sensory loss followed by severe neuropathic pain, sensory gating breakdown, or altered states of arousal.

name: Hypothalamus
function: Maintains homeostasis: controls hunger, thirst, body temperature, circadian sleep patterns, autonomic functions, and memory/emotion via chemical signaling to the pituitary gland.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Disrupted thermoregulation, severe hyperphagia/aphagia, diabetes insipidus, disrupted sleep-wake cycles, and emotional labileness.

name: Pituitary Gland ('Master Gland')
function: Pea-sized structure governing other glands; regulates hormone flow for thyroid, adrenals, ovaries, and testicles based on hypothalamic chemical signals via its stalk.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Systemic hormonal imbalances, Cushing's disease, acromegaly, or bitemporal hemianopia (due to optic chiasm compression above it).

name: Pineal Gland
function: Responds to light/dark cycles and secretes melatonin to regulate circadian rhythms and the sleep-wake cycle.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Severe sleep disruption, delayed sleep phase syndrome, or Parinaud syndrome (vertical gaze palsy) if pineal tumors compress the tectum.

name: Amygdala
function: Regulates core emotions (particularly fear, threat responses, 'fight or flight'), emotional memory, stress, and reward processing.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Loss of fear conditioning, hyperorality, hypersexuality, psychic blindness, and extreme emotional unresponsiveness to threat.

name: Hippocampus & Hippocampal Formation
function: Converts short-term experiences into lasting long-term declarative memories; supports learning, spatial navigation, and spatial perception.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Inability to consolidate new episodic/semantic memories (e.g., Patient H.M. profile), disorientation in space, and early vulnerability in Alzheimer's disease.

name: Basal Ganglia (Striatum, Globus Pallidus, Subthalamic Nucleus)
function: Fine-tunes voluntary motor movements, gates motor initiation, regulates habit formation, and supports procedural motor learning.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Hypokinetic symptoms (resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity) or hyperkinetic choreiform movements and involuntary motor bursts.

name: Ventricular System & Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)
function: Four open internal cavities that manufacture CSF; circulates fluid around central nervous system to cushion brain/spinal cord, deliver nutrients, and remove waste.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: CSF blockage leading to ventricular expansion, headache, papilledema, cognitive slowing, gait ataxia, and urinary incontinence.

name: Meninges (Dura Mater, Arachnoid Mater, Pia Mater)
function: Three protective membranes surrounding CNS: Dura (tough outer double-layer with venous sinuses), Arachnoid (weblike tissue over subarachnoid CSF space), and Pia (richly vascularized membrane hugging brain contours).

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity, photophobia), or intracranial hemorrhage causing mass effect and uncal herniation.

name: Cerebral Blood Supply (Carotid, Vertebral, Circle of Willis)
function: Delivers oxygenated blood via Internal Carotids (front portion) and Vertebral/Basilar Arteries (rear portion); joined by the Circle of Willis loop at the base for collateral circulation.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Focal neurological deficits depending on arterial territory (e.g., MCA stroke causing facial droop and arm weakness; PCA stroke causing visual field loss).

name: Cranial Nerves (CN I to XII)
function: 12 pairs: CN I (Olfactory/Smell) & CN II (Optic/Sight) emerge from cerebrum; CN III-XII emerge from brainstem handling eye movement (III, IV, VI), jaw/face sensation & chewing (V), face motor/taste (VII), balance/hearing (VIII), throat/taste (IX), heart/viscera/digestion (X), neck/shoulders (XI), and tongue (XII).

clinicalDeficit.condition: Cranial Neuropathies (e.g., Bell's Palsy, Trigeminal Neuralgia)
clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Anosmia (CN I), blindness/visual cut (CN II), diplopia/ptosis (CN III, IV, VI), facial numbness/tic (CN V), facial paralysis (CN VII), vertigo/hearing loss (CN VIII), dysphagia (CN IX, X), or tongue deviation (CN XII).

name: Cerebellum
function: Coordinates fine motor skills, precision movement timing, posture control, and balance.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Gait instability (wide-based gait), dysmetria (past-pointing), dysdiadochokinesia, and intention tremors during voluntary movement.

name: Brainstem (Midbrain, Pons, Medulla Oblongata)
function: Manages involuntary life-sustaining tasks (breathing, heart rate, swallowing, blood pressure) and acts as the origin point for Cranial Nerves III through XII.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Pontine damage causes total quadriplegia with eye movement preservation (Locked-in); medullary damage is rapidly fatal due to respiratory failure.

name: Central Sulcus & Motor Hand Omega Area
function: Divides frontal and parietal lobes. Features a distinct inverted 'Omega' shape on the lateral aspect representing hand motor (precentral) and somatosensory (postcentral) control. Shows structural motor lateralization based on handedness.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Isolated loss of motor control, weakness, or tactile discrimination specifically in the contralateral hand.

name: Calcarine Sulcus (Primary Visual Cortex - V1)
function: Receives initial retinotopic visual inputs from the LGN. Acts as the primary gateway for conscious visual perception.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Loss of vision in the contralateral visual field with macular sparing if collateral circulation is intact.

name: Ventral Temporal Visual Stream ('What' Pathway)
function: Processes visual information streaming from V1 down the inferior temporal lobe to recognize complex shapes, places, objects, and faces (Fusiform Face Area).

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Inability to recognize familiar objects or faces visually, despite intact basic vision.

name: Area MT / V5 (Middle Temporal Area)
function: Enriched in direction-selective motion neurons. Specialized for processing visual motion ('building our notion of motion').

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Inability to perceive continuous fluid movement; objects appear as a series of frozen freeze-frame snapshots.

name: Orbitofrontal Cortex (Phineas Gage Region)
function: Integrates visceral/emotional signals with decision-making, impulse control, social decorum, and risk reward assessment.

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Profound changes in personality, disinhibition, emotional apathy, impulsivity, and poor judgment (classical Phineas Gage presentation).

name: Cortical Pyramidal Neurons (Microanatomy)
function: Principal excitatory projection neurons of gray matter. Feature a pyramid-shaped soma, long apical dendrite extending to the surface, basal dendritic tree with spiny protrusions for synaptic input, and a long axon (conducting zone).

clinicalDeficit.symptoms: Loss of dendritic spines leads to synaptic disconnectivity seen in neurodegenerative conditions and cognitive decline.
